Below is a reference on the Dafny language and verifier, followed by your task.

=== DAFNY REFERENCE ===
# Dafny reference for verification work

Based on the Dafny Reference Manual (https://dafny.org/latest/DafnyRef/DafnyRef).
Section numbers in brackets point to the manual.

## 1. How Dafny verifies

- Dafny is **modular**: each method and function is verified on its own, using only the
  *specifications* (not the bodies) of the methods it calls. [13.6.1.3]
- A program is verified when every method and function verifies and there are no
  unproven assumptions (`assume` statements). [13.6.1.3]
- Specifications and ghost code are used only during verification; the compiler drops them. [1]
- Dafny first checks that each specification is **well-formed** on its own (no out-of-bounds
  index, null dereference or division by zero inside `requires`/`ensures`), then checks the body
  against the specification. These are reported as separate assertion batches. [7.8]

## 2. Contracts

| Clause | Meaning | Default when absent |
|---|---|---|
| `requires P` | Precondition. Checked at every call site; the body may assume it on entry. | `requires true` |
| `ensures Q` | Postcondition. Must hold on every return path. | `ensures true` |
| `modifies S` | Heap locations a method (or loop) may write. | Nothing (empty set) for methods |
| `reads S` | Heap locations a function may read. | Functions: nothing. Methods: anything (`*`) |
| `decreases E` | Termination measure for recursion or loops. | Dafny guesses (see §4) |

[7.1.1–7.1.6]

- Multiple `requires` (or `ensures`) clauses are **conjoined in order**. Order matters: an earlier
  conjunct can make a later one well-defined, e.g. `requires 0 < a.Length` before
  `requires a[0] == 0`. [7.1.1, 7.1.2]
- Clauses can be labeled: `requires L: 0 < i < 10`. [7.1.1]
- Framing applies only to the heap (objects and arrays). Local variables, `seq`, `set`,
  `multiset` and `map` are values and never appear in frames. [7.1.4]
- `modifies` means "may write". Writing a location not in the frame is an error even if
  the old value is restored later. Newly allocated objects may always be modified. [7.1.6]

```dafny
class Thermostat {
  var target: int
  var history: seq<int>

  method SetTarget(t: int)
    modifies this                                       // writes fields of this object
    ensures target == t
    ensures history == old(history) + [old(target)]    // old(...) = value on entry
  {
    history := history + [target];
    target := t;
  }
}
```

## 3. Loops

Multiple `invariant` clauses are conjoined in source order. [7.1.7]

For a loop `while G invariant I { Body }`, Dafny proves:

1. **I holds on entry**: it must be true just before the loop is first reached. [7.1.7, 8.15.1]
2. **I is maintained**: assuming `I && G` at the start of an iteration, `I` holds again after
   `Body`. [8.15.1]
3. **After the loop, Dafny knows only `I && !G`** (plus facts about variables the loop does
   not assign). Anything needed later, such as the method's postcondition, must follow from
   that. Dafny does not discover loop properties by itself. [8.15.1]

Other rules:

- Invariants are **not checked at `break`**. [8.15.4]
- **Loop targets**: local variables that the loop body never assigns are known to be unchanged.
  If the body may write the heap, the loop's effective `modifies` clause is the enclosing
  method's unless the loop declares its own. Add an invariant (or a narrower loop `modifies`)
  to keep facts about heap locations the loop does not touch. [8.15.3]

```dafny
method Clamp(a: array<int>, lo: int, hi: int)
  requires lo <= hi
  modifies a
  ensures forall k :: 0 <= k < a.Length ==> lo <= a[k] <= hi
  ensures forall k :: 0 <= k < a.Length && lo <= old(a[k]) <= hi ==> a[k] == old(a[k])
{
  var i := 0;
  while i < a.Length
    invariant 0 <= i <= a.Length                                    // bounds
    invariant forall k :: 0 <= k < i ==> lo <= a[k] <= hi           // done part: in range
    invariant forall k :: 0 <= k < i && lo <= old(a[k]) <= hi ==> a[k] == old(a[k])
    invariant forall k :: i <= k < a.Length ==> a[k] == old(a[k])   // rest: untouched
  {
    if a[i] < lo {
      a[i] := lo;
    } else if a[i] > hi {
      a[i] := hi;
    }
    i := i + 1;
  }
  // Here Dafny knows: invariants && !(i < a.Length), so i == a.Length.
}
```

Checks on this example:
- *On entry*: with `i == 0`, the bounds hold and the `0 <= k < 0` invariants are vacuously
  true; the "untouched" invariant holds because nothing has been written yet.
- *Maintained*: the body changes only `a[i]`, so the facts about `k < i` still hold, the new
  element `a[i]` is now in range (and unchanged if it already was), and the "untouched"
  invariant still covers `k >= i + 1`.
- *After the loop*: `i <= a.Length && !(i < a.Length)` gives `i == a.Length`, so the
  "done part" invariants become the postconditions. Without the upper bound `i <= a.Length`,
  this last step fails. Without the "untouched" invariant, the second postcondition fails,
  because Dafny would not know what `a[i]` held before the iteration that changed it.

## 4. Termination

- Every loop and recursive call needs a measure that **strictly decreases** and is **bounded
  below** (for integers, the bound is 0). [8.15.2]
- For a loop guard `i < n`, Dafny guesses `decreases n - i`. For recursion, it guesses the
  parameter list in order. [8.15.2, 7.1.3]
- Measures are lexicographic tuples: `decreases x, y`. [7.1.3]
- `decreases *` skips the termination proof (allowed for loops and compiled methods only,
  not for functions or lemmas); a method calling such code must be `decreases *` too. [7.1.3]
- Termination is its own check. It is separate from loop invariants and postconditions.

## 5. Types and collections

| Type | Key operations |
|---|---|
| `int`, `nat` | `nat` is `int` restricted to `0 <= n`. Division and `%` are Euclidean: `a % b` is never negative. No implicit `int`/`real` conversion; use `as int` / `as real`. |
| `seq<T>` | `|s|`, `s[i]`, `s[i := v]`, `s + t`, `x in s`, slices `s[lo..hi]`, `s[lo..]`, `s[..hi]`; `s[0..|s|] == s`; `<` / `<=` mean (proper) prefix. |
| `set<T>` | `x in s`, `x !in s`, `|s|`, `+` union, `-` difference, `*` intersection, `!!` disjoint. |
| `multiset<T>` | `m[x]` multiplicity, `+`, `-`, `*`, `|m|`; `multiset(s)` converts a sequence. |
| `map<K,V>` | `m[k]`, `m[k := v]`, `k in m`, `m.Keys`, `m.Values`, `m.Items`; `+` merges (right side wins). |
| `array<T>` | `a.Length`, `a[i]`, `new int[n]`. Arrays live on the heap and need `modifies`/`reads`. `a[..]`, `a[lo..hi]`, `a[lo..]`, `a[..hi]` give a `seq<T>` (requires `0 <= lo <= hi <= a.Length`). |

[5.5, 5.6.3.1, 5.10.2]

Common idioms:
- Permutation of an array: `multiset(a[..]) == multiset(old(a[..]))`.
- Sortedness: `forall i, j :: 0 <= i < j < a.Length ==> a[i] <= a[j]`.
- Quantifier bounds also act as well-formedness guards: `forall i :: 0 <= i < |s| ==> s[i] > 0`.

## 6. Two-state expressions

- `old(e)`: value of heap reads in `e` on method entry. It has no effect on locals or
  parameters. `old@L(e)` uses the state at label `L`. [9.22]
- `fresh(e)`: objects in `e` were allocated after method entry. [9.23]
- `unchanged(o)`: every field of `o` is equal to its value on entry. [9.25]

## 7. Functions, predicates, lemmas and proof statements

- **Functions** are pure; the body defines them, so a postcondition is usually not needed.
  **Predicates** are boolean functions. A `ghost` function or predicate exists only for
  verification. [6.3, 7.3]
- **Lemmas** are ghost methods used as proofs: `lemma L(x: T) requires P(x) ensures Q(x) { ... }`.
  Calling `L(x)` makes `Q(x)` available. Prefer `requires P ensures Q` over `ensures P ==> Q`. [6.3.3, 13.7.1.3]
- `assert P;` makes Dafny prove `P` at that point and then use it. Good for locating where a
  proof breaks. [8.17]
- `assert P by { ... }` proves `P` using the block's steps, then forgets them. [8.17]
- `assume P;` is accepted without proof and makes the program unsound; Dafny warns about it. [8.18]
- `forall x | P(x) ensures Q(x) { L(x); }` proves `forall x :: P(x) ==> Q(x)` from a lemma. [6.3]
- `calc == { A; B; { L(x); } C; }` writes a chain of equalities (or `<`, `<=`, `==>`, ...) with
  justifications. [8.23, 13.7.1.3]

### Worked proofs

**Induction with a lemma.** A recursive lemma call is the induction hypothesis.
Dafny checks that the lemma's `decreases` measure (here `n`) goes down.

```dafny
function Rep(x: int, n: nat): seq<int>
{
  if n == 0 then [] else [x] + Rep(x, n - 1)
}

lemma RepLength(x: int, n: nat)
  ensures |Rep(x, n)| == n
{
  if n > 0 {
    RepLength(x, n - 1);   // induction hypothesis for n - 1
  }
}
```

**A `calc` proof.** Each step is checked separately; the hint in braces is used for the step
it sits on.

```dafny
lemma RepAppend(x: int, n: nat, m: nat)
  ensures Rep(x, n + m) == Rep(x, n) + Rep(x, m)
{
  if n > 0 {
    calc == {
      Rep(x, n + m);
      [x] + Rep(x, (n - 1) + m);            // unfold the definition
      { RepAppend(x, n - 1, m); }           // induction hypothesis
      [x] + (Rep(x, n - 1) + Rep(x, m));
      ([x] + Rep(x, n - 1)) + Rep(x, m);    // concatenation is associative
      Rep(x, n) + Rep(x, m);                // fold the definition
    }
  }
}
```

**Using a lemma inside a loop with `assert ... by`.** The lemma's fact is needed only to
re-establish the invariant, so it is kept inside the `by` block.

```dafny
method Fill(x: int, n: nat) returns (s: seq<int>)
  ensures s == Rep(x, n)
{
  s := [];
  var i := 0;
  while i < n
    invariant 0 <= i <= n
    invariant s == Rep(x, i)
  {
    s := s + [x];
    assert s == Rep(x, i + 1) by {
      RepAppend(x, i, 1);   // Rep(x, i + 1) == Rep(x, i) + Rep(x, 1), and Rep(x, 1) == [x]
    }
    i := i + 1;
  }
}
```

**Permutation with `multiset`.** Swapping two elements keeps the multiset of the array, so
the permutation invariant is maintained automatically. The invariant `i % 2 == 0` is what
lets Dafny conclude, after the loop, that every pair was handled.

```dafny
method SwapPairs(a: array<int>)
  modifies a
  ensures multiset(a[..]) == multiset(old(a[..]))
  ensures forall k :: 0 <= k && k + 1 < a.Length && k % 2 == 0 ==> a[k] == old(a[k + 1]) && a[k + 1] == old(a[k])
{
  var i := 0;
  while i + 1 < a.Length
    invariant 0 <= i <= a.Length
    invariant i % 2 == 0
    invariant multiset(a[..]) == multiset(old(a[..]))
    invariant forall k :: 0 <= k < i && k % 2 == 0 ==> a[k] == old(a[k + 1]) && a[k + 1] == old(a[k])
    invariant forall k :: i <= k < a.Length ==> a[k] == old(a[k])
  {
    a[i], a[i + 1] := a[i + 1], a[i];
    i := i + 2;
  }
}
```

## 8. Reading verifier output

Each error line has the form `file.dfy(line,col): Error: message`. When a specification
clause is involved, a `Related location` line points at the clause that could not be proved.
Exact wording varies across Dafny versions ("might not hold" in older ones, "could not be
proved" in newer ones).

| Message | What failed |
|---|---|
| `a postcondition could not be proved on this return path` + `this is the postcondition that could not be proved` | An `ensures` clause does not follow from the state at that return. |
| `this loop invariant could not be proved on entry` | The invariant is false just before the loop. |
| `this invariant could not be proved to be maintained by the loop` | One iteration of the body does not re-establish the invariant. |
| `a precondition for this call could not be proved` + `this is the precondition that could not be proved` | A callee's `requires` clause is not established at the call. |
| `function precondition could not be proved` | A function is applied outside its `requires`. |
| `assertion might not hold` / `this proposition could not be proved` | An `assert` (or an internal assertion) cannot be proved. |
| `index out of range`, `lower bound out of range`, `upper bound below lower bound or above length of ...` | An index or slice may be out of bounds, possibly inside a specification. |
| `decreases expression might not decrease`, `decreases expression must be bounded below by 0`, `this decreases clause was not satisfied` | Termination. |
| `value does not satisfy the subset constraints of 'nat'` | A value may be negative where a `nat` is required. |
| `possible division by zero` | A divisor may be 0. |

Messages such as `arguments to > must be of a numeric type ...` or
`first argument to && must be of type bool` are **type errors**, reported before verification.
The program must type-check before any of the checks above run.

## 9. Debugging a failing proof

The manual's method is to turn the failure into an `assert` and move it backwards (computing the
weakest precondition) until the problem is obvious. [13.7.1]

1. **Failing postcondition**: replace `return e;` with `r := e; return;`, then add
   `assert <postcondition>;` just before the return. The error moves to the `assert`.
2. **Move the assert up** through statements:

| Code after the failing point | Assert before it |
|---|---|
| `x := Y; assert P;` | `assert P[x := Y];` |
| `if B { assert P; ... }` | `assert B ==> P;` |
| `if B { ... } else { assert P; ... }` | `assert !B ==> P;` |
| `var x := m(k); assert P(x);` (with `m` requires `A`, ensures `B`) | `assert A(k); assert forall x :: B(k, x) ==> P(x);` |

3. **Split** compound goals: `assert A && B;` into `assert A; assert B;`, and
   `assert A ==> B;` into `if A { assert B; }`.
4. **Quantifiers**: prove `forall x :: P(x) ==> Q(x)` with
   `forall x | P(x) ensures Q(x) { assert Q(x); }`. For `exists`, assert the property for a
   concrete witness first: `assert P(x0);`.
5. **For loops**, check the three obligations in §3 separately: assert the invariant just before
   the loop, assert it at the end of the body, and assert the postcondition right after the loop.

[13.7.1.1–13.7.1.3]

**Counterexamples**: `--extract-counterexample` reports a possible counterexample as a set of
assumptions about variable values. Dafny cannot guarantee that it actually violates the assertion,
so treat it as a hint. [13.7.1.4]

## 10. Command line

```
dafny verify program.dfy
dafny verify --extract-counterexample program.dfy     # report a potential counterexample
dafny verify --verification-time-limit 30 program.dfy # seconds per verification attempt
dafny verify --isolate-assertions program.dfy         # verify each assertion in its own batch
```

[13.6.1.3, 13.9.7]

For slow or timing-out proofs: `assume false;` at a point stops verification there, which helps
find the expensive part (remove it afterwards). `assert P by { ... }` keeps helper facts from
slowing down later proofs. [13.7.2]
=== END OF DAFNY REFERENCE ===

=== PROGRAM ===
/* https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-palindromic-substring/
Given a string s, return the longest palindromic substring in s.

Example 1:
Input: s = "babad"
Output: "bab"
Explanation: "aba" is also a valid answer.
*/


// Specifying the problem: whether `s[i..j]` is palindromic
ghost predicate palindromic(s: string, i: int, j: int)
  requires 0 <= i <= j <= |s|
  decreases j - i
{
  j - i < 2 || (s[i] == s[j-1] && palindromic(s, i+1, j-1))
}

// A "common sense" about palindromes:
lemma lemma_palindromic_contains(s: string, lo: int, hi: int, lo': int, hi': int)
  requires 0 <= lo <= lo' <= hi' <= hi <= |s|
  requires lo + hi == lo' + hi'
  requires palindromic(s, lo, hi)
  ensures palindromic(s, lo', hi')
  decreases lo' - lo
{
  if lo < lo' {
    lemma_palindromic_contains(s, lo + 1, hi - 1, lo', hi');
  }
}

// A useful "helper function" that returns the longest palindrome at a given center (i0, j0).
method expand_from_center(s: string, i0: int, j0: int) returns (lo: int, hi: int)
  requires 0 <= i0 <= j0 <= |s|
  requires palindromic(s, i0, j0)
  ensures 0 <= lo <= hi <= |s| && palindromic(s, lo, hi)
  ensures forall i, j | 0 <= i <= j <= |s| && palindromic(s, i, j)  // Among all palindromes
    && i + j == i0 + j0                                             // sharing the same center,
    :: j - i <= hi - lo                                             // `s[lo..hi]` is longest.
{
  lo, hi := i0, j0;

  // we try expanding whenever possible:
  while lo - 1 >= 0 && hi < |s| && s[lo - 1] == s[hi]
    invariant 0 <= lo <= hi <= |s| && lo + hi == i0 + j0
    invariant palindromic(s, lo, hi)
  {
    lo, hi := lo - 1, hi + 1;
  }

  // proves that we cannot go further:
  forall i, j | 0 <= i <= j <= |s| && i + j == i0 + j0 && j - i > hi - lo ensures !palindromic(s, i, j) {
    if palindromic(s, i, j) { // prove by contradiction:
      lemma_palindromic_contains(s, i, j, lo - 1, hi + 1);
    }
  }
}


// The main algorithm.
// We traverse all centers from left to right, and "expand" each of them, to find the longest palindrome.
method longestPalindrome(s: string) returns (ans: string, lo: int, hi: int)
  ensures 0 <= lo <= hi <= |s| && ans == s[lo..hi]  // `ans` is indeed a substring in `s`
  ensures palindromic(s, lo, hi)  // `ans` is palindromic
  ensures forall i, j | 0 <= i <= j <= |s| && palindromic(s, i, j) :: j - i <= hi - lo  // `ans` is longest
{
  lo, hi := 0, 0;
  for k := 0 to |s|
    invariant 0 <= lo <= hi <= |s|
    invariant palindromic(s, lo, hi)
    invariant forall i, j | 0 <= i <= j <= |s| && i + j < 2 * k && palindromic(s, i, j) :: j - i <= hi - lo
  {
    var a, b := expand_from_center(s, k, k);
    if b - a > hi - lo {
      lo, hi := a, b;
    }
    var c, d := expand_from_center(s, k, k + 1);
    if d - c > hi - lo {
      lo, hi := c, d;
    }
  }
  return s[lo..hi], lo, hi;
}


/* Discussions
1. Dafny is super bad at slicing (esp. nested slicing).
  Do circumvent it whenever possible. It can save you a lot of assertions & lemmas!

  For example, instead of `palindromic(s[i..j])`, use the pattern `palindromic(s, i, j)` instead.
  I didn't realize this (ref: https://github.com/Nangos/dafleet/commit/3302ddd7642240ff2b2f6a8c51e8becd5c9b6437),
  Resulting in a couple of clumsy lemmas.

2. Bonus -- Manacher's algorithm
  Our above solution needs `O(|s|^2)` time in the worst case. Can we improve it? Yes.

  Manacher's algorithm guarantees an `O(|s|)` time.
  To get the intuition, ask yourself: when will it really take `O(|s|^2)` time?
  When there are a lot of "nesting and overlapping" palindromes. like in `abcbcbcba` or even `aaaaaa`.

  Imagine each palindrome as a "mirror". "Large mirrors" reflect "small mirrors".
  Therefore, when we "expand" from some "center", we can "reuse" some information from its "mirrored center".
  For example, we move the "center", from left to right, in the string `aiaOaia...`
  Here, the char `O` is the "large mirror".
  When the current center is the second `i`, it is "mirrored" to the first `i` (which we've calculated for),
  so we know the palindrome centered at the second `i` must have at least a length of 3 (`aia`).
  So we can expand directly from `aia`, instead of expanding from scratch.

  Manacher's algorithm is verified below.
  Also, I will verify that "every loop is entered for only `O(|s|)` times",
  which "indirectly" proves that the entire algorithm runs in `O(|s|)` time.
*/


// A reference implementation of Manacher's algorithm:
// (Ref. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longest_palindromic_substring#Manacher's_algorithm) for details...
method {:vcs_split_on_every_assert} longestPalindrome'(s: string) returns (ans: string, lo: int, hi: int)
  ensures 0 <= lo <= hi <= |s| && ans == s[lo..hi]
  ensures palindromic(s, lo, hi)
  ensures forall i, j | 0 <= i <= j <= |s| && palindromic(s, i, j) :: j - i <= hi - lo
{
  var bogus: char :| true;  // an arbitrary character
  var s' := insert_bogus_chars(s, bogus);
  var radii := new int[|s'|];
  var center, radius := 0, 0;
  // vars below are just for verifying time complexity:
  ghost var loop_counter_outer, loop_counter_inner1, loop_counter_inner2 := 0, 0, 0;

  while center < |s'|
    invariant 0 <= center <= |s'|
    invariant forall c | 0 <= c < center :: max_radius(s', c, radii[c])
    invariant center < |s'| ==> inbound_radius(s', center, radius) && palindromic_radius(s', center, radius)
    invariant center == |s'| ==> radius == 0
    invariant loop_counter_outer <= center
    invariant loop_counter_inner1 <= center + radius && loop_counter_inner2 <= (center) + 1
  {
    loop_counter_outer := loop_counter_outer + 1;

    // Stage 1: Still the normal "expand from center" routine, except `radius` is NOT necessarily zero:
    while center - (radius + 1) >= 0 && center + (radius + 1) < |s'|
        && s'[center - (radius + 1)] == s'[center + (radius + 1)]
      decreases center - radius
      invariant inbound_radius(s', center, radius) && palindromic_radius(s', center, radius)
      invariant loop_counter_inner1 <= center + radius
    {
      loop_counter_inner1 := loop_counter_inner1 + 1;
      radius := radius + 1;
    }
    lemma_end_of_expansion(s', center, radius);

    radii[center] := radius;
    var old_center, old_radius := center, radius;
    center := center + 1;
    radius := 0;

    // Stage 2: Quickly infer the maximal radius, using the symmetry of known palindromes. 
    while center <= old_center + old_radius
      invariant 0 <= center <= |s'|
      invariant forall c | 0 <= c < center :: max_radius(s', c, radii[c])
      invariant center < |s'| ==> inbound_radius(s', center, radius) && palindromic_radius(s', center, radius)
      invariant loop_counter_inner2 <= center - 1
    {
      loop_counter_inner2 := loop_counter_inner2 + 1;

      var mirrored_center := old_center - (center - old_center);
      var max_mirrored_radius := old_center + old_radius - center;
      lemma_mirrored_palindrome(s', old_center, old_radius, mirrored_center, radii[mirrored_center], center);

      if radii[mirrored_center] < max_mirrored_radius {
        radii[center] := radii[mirrored_center];
        center := center + 1;
      } else if radii[mirrored_center] > max_mirrored_radius {
        radii[center] := max_mirrored_radius;
        center := center + 1;
      } else {
        radius := max_mirrored_radius;
        break;
      }
    }
  }
  // verify that the worst time complexity (measured by loop iterations) is O(|s'|) == O(|s|):
  assert |s'| == 2 * |s| + 1;
  assert loop_counter_outer <= |s'|;
  assert loop_counter_inner1 <= |s'|;
  assert loop_counter_inner2 <= |s'|; 

  // wrap up results:
  var (c, r) := argmax(radii, 0);
  lo, hi := (c - r) / 2, (c + r) / 2; // notice that both ends are bogus chars at position 0, 2, 4, 6, etc.!
  lemma_result_transfer(s, s', bogus, radii, c, r, hi, lo);
  return s[lo..hi], lo, hi;        
}


// Below are helper functions and lemmas we used:

// Inserts bogus characters to the original string (e.g. from `abc` to `|a|b|c|`).
// Note that this is neither efficient nor necessary in reality, but just for the ease of understanding.
function {:opaque} insert_bogus_chars(s: string, bogus: char): (s': string)

ghost predicate inbound_radius(s': string, c: int, r: int)
{

  requires inbound_radius(s', c, r)

}

// Whether `r` is the maximal palindromic radius at center `c`.

{
  && inbound_radius(s', c, r)
  && palindromic_radius(s', c, r)
  && (forall r' | r' > r && inbound_radius(s', c, r') :: !palindromic_radius(s', c, r'))

{

}

// When "expand from center" ends, we've find the max radius:
lemma lemma_end_of_expansion(s': string, c: int, r: int)
  requires inbound_radius(s', c, r) && palindromic_radius(s', c, r)
  requires inbound_radius(s', c, r + 1) ==> s'[c - (r + 1)] != s'[c + (r + 1)]
  ensures max_radius(s', c, r)
{
  forall r' | r' > r && inbound_radius(s', c, r') ensures !palindromic_radius(s', c, r') {
    if palindromic_radius(s', c, r') {  // proof by contradiction

    }
  }
}

// The critical insight behind Manacher's algorithm.
//
// Given the longest palindrome centered at `c` has length `r`, consider the interval from `c-r` to `c+r`.
// Consider a pair of centers in the interval: `c1` (left half) and `c2` (right half), equally away from `c`.
// Then, the length of longest palindromes at `c1` and `c2` are related as follows:
lemma lemma_mirrored_palindrome(s': string, c: int, r: int, c1: int, r1: int, c2: int)
  requires max_radius(s', c, r) && max_radius(s', c1, r1)
  requires c - r <= c1 < c < c2 <= c + r
  requires c2 - c == c - c1
  ensures c2 + r1 < c + r ==> max_radius(s', c2, r1)
  ensures c2 + r1 > c + r ==> max_radius(s', c2, c + r - c2)
  ensures c2 + r1 == c + r ==> palindromic_radius(s', c2, c + r - c2)
{
  // proof looks long, but is quite straightforward at each step:
  if c2 + r1 < c + r {
    for r2 := 0 to r1
      invariant palindromic_radius(s', c2, r2)
    {
      var r2' := r2 + 1;
      assert s'[c1+r2'] == s'[c2-r2'] by { lemma_palindromic_radius_contains(s', c, r, abs(c - c1 - r2')); }
      assert s'[c1-r2'] == s'[c2+r2'] by { lemma_palindromic_radius_contains(s', c, r, abs(c - c1 + r2')); }
      assert s'[c1-r2'] == s'[c1+r2'] by { lemma_palindromic_radius_contains(s', c1, r1, r2'); }
    }
    var r2' := r1 + 1;
    assert s'[c1+r2'] == s'[c2-r2'] by { lemma_palindromic_radius_contains(s', c, r, abs(c - c1 - r2')); }
    assert s'[c1-r2'] == s'[c2+r2'] by { lemma_palindromic_radius_contains(s', c, r, abs(c - c1 + r2')); }
    assert s'[c1-r2'] != s'[c1+r2'] by { assert !palindromic_radius(s', c1, r2'); }
    lemma_end_of_expansion(s', c2, r1);
  } else {
    for r2 := 0 to c + r - c2
      invariant palindromic_radius(s', c2, r2)
    {
      var r2' := r2 + 1;
      assert s'[c1+r2'] == s'[c2-r2'] by { lemma_palindromic_radius_contains(s', c, r, abs(c - c1 - r2')); }
      assert s'[c1-r2'] == s'[c2+r2'] by { lemma_palindromic_radius_contains(s', c, r, abs(c - c1 + r2')); }

        assert s'[c1-r2'] != s'[c2+r2'] by { assert !palindromic_radius(s', c, r + 1); }
        assert s'[c1-r2'] == s'[c1+r2'] by { lemma_palindromic_radius_contains(s', c1, r1, r2'); }
        lemma_end_of_expansion(s', c2, c + r - c2);
      }
    }
  }
}
//, where:
ghost function abs(x: int): int {
  if x >= 0 then x else -x
}

// Transfering our final result on `s'` to that on `s`:
lemma lemma_result_transfer(s: string, s': string, bogus: char, radii: array<int>, c: int, r: int, hi: int, lo: int)
  requires s' == insert_bogus_chars(s, bogus)
  requires radii.Length == |s'|
  requires forall i | 0 <= i < radii.Length :: max_radius(s', i, radii[i])
  requires (c, r) == argmax(radii, 0)
  requires lo == (c - r) / 2 && hi == (c + r) / 2
  ensures 0 <= lo <= hi <= |s|
  ensures palindromic(s, lo, hi)
  ensures forall i, j | 0 <= i <= j <= |s| && palindromic(s, i, j) :: j - i <= hi - lo
{
  // For each center, rephrase [maximal radius in `s'`] into [maximal interval in `s`]:
  forall k | 0 <= k < radii.Length
  ensures max_interval_for_same_center(s, k, (k - radii[k]) / 2, (k + radii[k]) / 2) {
    // We need to show `k` and `radii[k]` are either "both odd" or "both even". We prove by contradiction:
    if (k + radii[k]) % 2 == 1 {
      lemma_palindrome_bogus(s, s', bogus, k, radii[k]);
    }
    // We then relate `s` and `s'` using their "isomorphism":
    var lo, hi := (k - radii[k]) / 2, (k + radii[k]) / 2;
    lemma_palindrome_isomorph(s, s', bogus, lo, hi);
    forall i, j | 0 <= i <= j <= |s| && i + j == k && j - i > radii[k] ensures !palindromic(s, i, j) {
      lemma_palindrome_isomorph(s, s', bogus, i, j);
    }
  }

  // We then iteratively build the last post-condition: 
  for k := 0 to radii.Length - 1
    invariant forall i, j | 0 <= i <= j <= |s| && palindromic(s, i, j) && i + j <= k :: j - i <= hi - lo
  {
    forall i, j | 0 <= i <= j <= |s| && palindromic(s, i, j) && i + j == k + 1 ensures j - i <= hi - lo {
      var k := k + 1;
      assert max_interval_for_same_center(s, k, (k - radii[k]) / 2, (k + radii[k]) / 2);
    }
  }
}

// The following returns whether `s[lo..hi]` is the longest palindrome s.t. `lo + hi == k`:
ghost predicate max_interval_for_same_center(s: string, k: int, lo: int, hi: int) {
  && 0 <= lo <= hi <= |s|
  && lo + hi == k
  && palindromic(s, lo, hi)
  && (forall i, j | 0 <= i <= j <= |s| && palindromic(s, i, j) && i + j == k :: j - i <= hi - lo)
}

// Establishes the "palindromic isomorphism" between `s` and `s'`.
lemma lemma_palindrome_isomorph(s: string, s': string, bogus: char, lo: int, hi: int)
  requires s' == insert_bogus_chars(s, bogus)
  requires 0 <= lo <= hi <= |s| 
  ensures palindromic(s, lo, hi) <==> palindromic_radius(s', lo + hi, hi - lo)
{
  if palindromic(s, lo, hi) {  // ==>
    for r := 0 to hi - lo
      invariant palindromic_radius(s', lo + hi, r)
    {
      if (lo + hi - r) % 2 == 1 {
        lemma_palindrome_bogus(s, s', bogus, lo + hi, r);
      } else {  
        var i', j' := lo + hi - (r + 1), lo + hi + (r + 1);
        var i, j := i' / 2, j' / 2;
        assert s[i] == s[j] by { lemma_palindromic_contains(s, lo, hi, i, j + 1); }
        // Notice that `s'[i'] == s[i] && s'[j'] == s[j]`; apparently Dafny does
      }
    }
  }
  if palindromic_radius(s', lo + hi, hi - lo) {  // <==
    var lo', hi' := lo, hi;
    while lo' + 1 <= hi' - 1
      invariant lo <= lo' <= hi' <= hi
      invariant lo' + hi' == lo + hi
      invariant palindromic_radius(s', lo + hi, hi' - lo')
      invariant palindromic(s, lo', hi') ==> palindromic(s, lo, hi)  // "reversed construction"
    {
      assert palindromic_radius(s', lo + hi, hi' - lo' - 1);  // ignore bogus chars and move on
      lo', hi' := lo' + 1, hi' - 1;
    }
  }
}

// Implies that whenever `c + r` is odd, the corresponding palindrome can be "lengthened for free"
// because its both ends are the bogus char.
lemma lemma_palindrome_bogus(s: string, s': string, bogus: char, c: int, r: int)
  requires s' == insert_bogus_chars(s, bogus)
  requires inbound_radius(s', c, r) && palindromic_radius(s', c, r)
  requires (c + r) % 2 == 1
  ensures inbound_radius(s', c, r + 1) && palindromic_radius(s', c, r + 1)
{
  var left, right := c - (r + 1), c + (r + 1);
  assert left == (left / 2) * 2;
  assert right == (right / 2) * 2;
  assert s'[left] == s'[right] == bogus;
}
